title: A Preregistered Audit of Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks: Preregistration→Execution Reconciliation and Lessons from a Degenerate Paired Run
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit to test whether conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized-token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) flag items in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample and whether applying preregistered guarded exclusions changes validator‑measured success rates. The preregistered estimand was the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) analyzed with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Execution produced a degenerate outcome: all 150 paired episodes passed the deterministic verifier in both baseline and guarded conditions (n11 = 150; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding an estimate of 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0). Crucially, artifact evidence shows two preregistration→execution facts that rendered the primary confirmatory test uninformative for contamination in web‑sourced corpora: (1) the executed sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), and (2) the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false in execution/model_configuration.json), so a single model generation per item was reused across conditions when no high‑confidence flags occurred (model_calls_used = 150). We formally record this preregistration→execution deviation, explain why the run is degenerate for detecting public‑benchmark leakage, document an implementation choice that suppressed persistence of full per‑item fuzzy‑overlap tables when no threshold crossings occurred (execution/transformation_manifest.json), and provide concrete, artifact‑anchored recommendations—provenance‑rich public sampling, independent per‑condition generations, full per‑item overlap persistence, multi‑model replication, and paraphrase‑robust detectors—to make future audits sensitive to contamination. All analysis artifacts and validator traces are archived in the execution bundle (see Disclosure Statement).

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated repair. Benchmark results influence operational trust and decisions, so evaluations must distinguish genuine model capability from benchmark contamination (items or templated prompts appearing in model training data) or construct invalidity (overly templated, low‑complexity items). Recent meta‑analyses and system papers call for contamination‑aware, oracle‑backed evaluations and preregistered audits that (a) define detectors and exclusion policies up front, (b) lock sampling and analysis plans, and (c) archive deterministic artifacts for independent verification. This work preregistered such an audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) and executed it end‑to‑end using a deterministic validator oracle (deterministic_netops_validator_v5).
sections.related_work: Empirical studies and benchmarks show that LLMs can produce useful network configurations and plausible repairs, but that naive generation sometimes introduces regressions; combining LLMs with validators or iterative generate–validate–repair loops improves average safety. Formal verification and static analysis techniques (e.g., Header Space Analysis and localized subspecification) are viable oracles for reachability and policy correctness and are commonly deployed in NetOps generate–validate pipelines. Separately, survey and methodological literature documents contamination and construct‑validity risks in LLM benchmarks and recommends deterministic fingerprinting, fuzzy n‑gram overlap, provenance tracing, and transparent reporting of detector outputs. Our audit implements a conservative subset of these defenses and focuses on an artifact‑grounded preregistration→execution reconciliation rather than proposing novel detectors.
sections.methodology: Preregistration summary. We preregistered the confirmatory estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), an exact McNemar two‑sided test as the primary test, paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for descriptive uncertainty, conservative contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap with preregistered high‑confidence threshold ≥0.80; and provenance timestamp heuristics), guarded exclusion rules (exclude and deterministically replace only high‑confidence flagged items), and deterministic sampling rules (task_count = 150 with fixed generator seeds). The preregistration listed an explicit benchmark_scope of four public datasets (OpenAlex identifiers): https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W4404602270, https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660. The preregistration and analysis plan are archived with the execution bundle.
sections.results: Execution and deterministic reconciliation. The pipeline executed to completion (planned_episode_count = 300; completed_episode_count = 300) with zero failed episodes. Due to shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false recorded in execution/model_configuration.json), the pipeline used a single model generation per item and reused it across baseline and guarded conditions when no high‑confidence exclusions were triggered; provider accounting shows model_calls_used = 150. Contamination detectors produced zero preregistered high‑confidence flags for the executed sample (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). The deterministic validator accepted all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150) and all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. Primary estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Representative per‑episode validator traces and raw responses are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json).
sections.discussion: Preregistration→execution deviation and formal reclassification. The preregistration targeted public datasets (listed OpenAlex IDs above) and allowed either independent per‑condition generation or shared generation semantics. The executed run sampled provenance‑stable synthetic tasks produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; every manifest entry carries source_identifier values with the prefix "synthetic-netops:" (e.g., see execution/task_manifest.jsonl representative entries). This choice—together with independent_condition_generation = false—made the prespecified primary confirmatory test uninformative for detecting contamination in web‑sourced corpora: when a single canonical model response is reused across baseline and guarded episodes, discordant pairs cannot arise unless exclusions trigger replacements. We therefore formally record this preregistration→execution deviation and reclassify the primary confirmatory test as degenerate under the executed configuration. The artifact evidence supporting this reclassification includes execution/task_manifest.jsonl (task provenance and generator seeds) and execution/model_configuration.json (independent_condition_generation = false and declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini").
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an artifact‑anchored audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluations. The run produced a degenerate paired outcome (complete concordant passes) because the executed sample was provenance‑stable synthetic content and the pipeline reused a single shared generation per item. This outcome does not imply absence of contamination in public web‑sourced benchmarks. From the archived evidence we recommend concrete, implementable changes to increase audit sensitivity: (1) sample provenance‑rich public items (URLs/DOIs/timestamps) so provenance heuristics are meaningful; (2) enable independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded outputs are independently realized; (3) persist full per‑item fuzzy 5‑gram overlap scores to enable threshold‑sensitivity reporting; (4) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to raise power to detect modest paired differences; and (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and targeted human adjudication for borderline cases. All recommended changes are implementable within the existing execution framework and are supported by the archived execution artifacts described above. Future preregistered runs that adopt these changes should yield non‑degenerate paired comparisons when contamination or templated leakage exists in sampled items. The execution bundle (model configuration, task manifest, raw responses, validator traces, analysis artifacts) is archived and described in the Disclosure Statement below.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Executed sample provenance was synthetic/deterministically generated (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"); absence of high‑confidence flags here does not imply absence of contamination in independent public, web‑sourced benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), which reuses a single generation per item across conditions and made the paired test uninformative for generation‑level contamination absent exclusions.

Contamination detection relied on conservative lexical heuristics (exact matches and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); paraphrased memorization or partial leakage may escape these detectors and require paraphrase‑robust methods or human adjudication.

Passing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates the checked functional constraints were satisfied but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
